title: 'Our kids can't': The soft bigotry of low expectations
author: Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes tackles a phrase common in staffrooms — 'our kids can't do that' — arguing that even when spoken with genuine compassion, it functions as a soft form of discrimination that quietly rations opportunity from the students who most need it. Drawing on a talk by Bentleigh West Primary principal Sarah Asome, she frames explicit, systematic teaching not as an alternative to challenge but as the mechanism that makes challenge survivable, rejecting the caricature of high expectations as simply throwing children at hard work and hoping. Hughes is careful to represent the research on teacher-expectation effects accurately rather than overclaim it, noting that reviews find the 'Pygmalion effect' produces modest rather than miraculous outcomes — but that these modest effects are real and compound over time through the texts, questions, and feedback teachers actually deliver. Her sharpest point is about equity: she names specific groups — disadvantaged students, students with disability, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander pupils — who are most likely to have adults 'confuse sensitivity to barriers with certainty about limitations,' turning protective intentions into rationed opportunity. The essay's practical resolution is linguistic and pedagogical at once: replacing 'they can't' with 'they can't yet' converts a fixed judgment about a child into a concrete teaching problem — what specific knowledge or skill needs to be built next.
points: Hughes's central mechanism — lowered expectations 'leak into practice' through simpler texts, thinner questions, and reduced challenge, which then 'produces the evidence used to justify it' — describes a self-confirming cycle that explains how well-intentioned compassion becomes structural disadvantage.

Her explicit list of groups most likely to be underestimated (disadvantaged students, students with disability, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander pupils) turns an abstract argument about expectations into a concrete equity claim about which students actually bear the cost of 'soft bigotry.'

The reframe from 'they can't' to 'they can't yet' gives teachers an immediately usable linguistic and diagnostic tool: it converts a fixed judgment about a student's capability into an actionable question about what specific knowledge or skill still needs to be taught.
quotes: There is an excuse I hear in schools that troubles me every time: 'Our kids can't do that.' It sounds compassionate. Yet compassion without ambition can become something much less benign: the soft bigotry of low expectations.
But challenge without support is abandonment rather than ambition.
Teachers' expectations can influence the opportunities, questions, feedback, attention and intellectual challenge that pupils receive.

Expectations are important because they leak into practice. When we believe pupils cannot manage complex texts, we give them simpler ones. Eventually, the lowered expectation produces the evidence used to justify it.

Children from disadvantaged backgrounds, children with disability, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander pupils, and those who have previously struggled are most likely to encounter adults who confuse sensitivity to barriers with certainty about limitations. We tell ourselves that we are adapting to need when we may actually be rationing opportunity.
The crucial word is 'yet'. They cannot read this independently yet. What vocabulary, background knowledge and fluency must we build? 'Yet' converts a judgement into a teaching problem.

High expectations are not motivational posters. They are visible in the text we place in front of a child, the question we return to after an incorrect answer, the knowledge we refuse to withhold and the support we provide without embarrassment.
